data.content_ref: inline:The target's mechanism conflates two logically distinct Popperian concepts—corroboration (past test survival) and content (potential falsifiers)—to construct a non-inductive justification, but the conflation fails on either reading. The mechanism states: 'one must test the theory that has survived the hardest attempts, as it contains the most potential falsifiers.' The word 'as' asserts that past survival JUSTIFIES preference BECAUSE of high content. But 'has survived the hardest attempts' (corroboration) and 'contains the most potential falsifiers' (content/verisimilitude) are independent properties: a high-content theory may have survived only trivial tests; a low-content theory may have survived severe ones. If the preference rests on past survival of hard tests, then choosing that theory for future action or testing projects past performance forward—classic induction, exactly what the defense claims to avoid. If instead the preference rests on content (most potential falsifiers), then it depends on the coherence of comparative content/verisimilitude, which the target itself flags as an undischarged countercondition ('If the formal definition of verisimilitude remains incoherent (per Tichý/Miller), the comparison of better corroborated theories lacks logical footing'). The mechanism thus faces a dilemma: it smuggles induction through the 'survived hardest attempts' horn, or it collapses into the acknowledged countercondition through the 'most potential falsifiers' horn. The reframing therefore does not produce a non-inductive justification at all; it merely disguises the induction by sliding between two different criteria without acknowledging that neither independently suffices.
